kicker: Some problems stayed open for nearly a hundred years. In 2026, AI helped put forward solutions.
summary: AI has put forward solutions to problems that stood for decades. Right or not: a machine checks every step, people check the problem.

quiz.q: A solution has been checked by a machine step by step. Why do people still need to look again?
options: The machine can't tell if its problem matches the real one
The machine often gets the harder steps of a solution wrong
The machine only checks spelling and punctuation
The machine checks many times slower than people
quiz.explain: The machine checks each step very reliably. But if the problem written for it drifts from the real one, it still says yes.

well.label: The pebble well
well.art: Looking down into an old stone well with moss and ferns, a bucket hanging from a wooden beam; the moon runs an arc along the top and its beam lights the well's wall. Drag the moon over each pebble on the rim: it flips and drops to a ledge, 2025 high, 2026 deeper; Navier–Stokes hits the water and breaks the moon's reflection, the 722 drafts fall like rain, today the water stills with a carved ring, and mist lies at the bottom.
well.prompt: Drag the moon: drop the pebbles one by one
well.moonAria: Drag the moon, or use the ← → keys to move through the milestones

fact.text: OpenAI announced that an experimental model scored 35/42, gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO); three former IMO medallists graded it.
Gemini Deep Think scored 35/42, solving 5 of 6 problems; the IMO President confirmed it was a gold-medal score.
Mathematician Levent Alpöge (Anthropic), helped by the AI Claude, found an example showing the Jacobian conjecture (posed in 1939) is false.
fact.verifiedBy: Archive of Formal Proofs (checked in Isabelle)

fact.text: OpenAI says its AI proved that smooth water can “blow up” by itself — with a version rewritten so a machine can check every step.
OpenAI posted 722 draft solutions to maths problems; the company itself says some still contain errors.
The Clay Institute only considers a prize once a solution is published in a qualifying outlet, at least two years have passed, and mathematicians broadly accept it.

horizon.text: The Math & AI advisory group at the IAS (Princeton): the future of mathematics cannot just be sitting and understanding results produced by AI companies.

insight.text: One year: from a school competition (07/2025) to a conjecture left open for 87 years (07/2026).

well.legend: ◇ the company's own claim · ● checked by someone outside

vortex.label: Water that blows up
vortex.art: A round pond under the moon seen three-quarter, a ring of mossy stones on raked sand, fireflies circling the bank — each one an AI copy running on its own (an agent). Swirl the pond and let go: the water calms by itself. Release the swarm: they spread out trying swirls, one tightens by itself into a funnel and the camera sinks toward the water until the far ridges rise; at the bottom the core flares into one point, a shockwave runs out and the agents line up into a stair of light climbing out of the pond.
vortex.prompt: Swirl the pond, then let go
vortex.stirAria: Swirl the pond: drag in a circle or hold an arrow key, then let go
steps: Release the AI swarm to search
vortex.releaseAria: Release the AI swarm to search for a swirl that tightens by itself
vortex.fireflies: Each firefly: one AI copy running on its own (an agent). About 10,000 copies, 88 hours.

insight.text: Can smooth water “blow up” by itself? OpenAI says 10,000 AI copies searched for 88 hours and found a way it can.

detail.text: Another team (Buckmaster, NYU, and Alpöge, Anthropic) posted a near-identical result about 12 hours earlier. Both built on the approach of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa (2023). The Clay Institute has not awarded the prize.

mason.label: The mason who tests every step
mason.art: A stone stair climbs the moonlit hillside, one step of the solution written for the machine cut into each stair; tapped in order, the old stonemason climbs to it and strikes it with his hammer. On the landing, under a paper lantern, a wooden sign carries the problem as written for the machine; beside it hangs the scroll with the original problem, to drag up and compare.
steps: Drag the original scroll up to the sign
mason.compare: Compare the sign with the original
mason.compareAria: Compare the problem written for the machine with the original problem
lines: For the machine: a even, b even
mason.original: Original: the sum of two odd numbers is even
mason.mismatch: The original says odd numbers; the problem for the machine says even. The machine checked correctly — but a different problem.

codeNote.text: The steps are a small example AI Zen wrote for illustration, not taken from a real proof.

insights.text: The machine checks one step at a time. Any wrong step, it stops right there.
The machine can check every step. Whether the problem itself is right, a person has to check.

detail.text: The checking tool here is called Lean. The Jacobian solution was checked again by another team with a second tool, Isabelle.

circle.label: Four chimes
circle.art: A stone well with a thick curb, the moon in its water; above it a square frame of wooden posts, a polished black stone chime hanging from each beam. Strike a chime and it swings, rings and sends a train of ripples across the well; the speaker's words appear on a hanging paper strip. When all four have rung, the ripples meet in the middle and cancel, the water stills and holds the whole moon.

view.text: This is “a significant event in mathematics” — but the future of mathematics cannot just be sitting and understanding results produced by AI companies.

common.text: A solution made by AI raises three questions: is it right, whose credit is it, and what is left for people to do.

quanta-ns.title: AI Has Solved One of Math's $1 Million Millennium Prize Problems
quanta-ns.note: Independent reporting; the agent counts, run times and costs are OpenAI's own figures. The article says the result is still contested and people must still check the problem statement in Lean.

datacamp-ns.title: Did AI Solve Navier-Stokes? OpenAI's Claim, Explained
datacamp-ns.note: Secondary source: OpenAI published a 166-page manuscript and the Lean version on 8 September and said it does not plan to accept the prize. The original page openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/ blocks lookup tools, so it has not been opened directly.

clay-rules.title: Millennium Prize Problems — Rules
clay-rules.note: Conditions for the prize: published in a qualifying outlet, at least two years' wait, and broad acceptance by the mathematical community.

aa-openai-math.title: OpenAI releases findings on hundreds of math problems
aa-openai-math.publisher: Anadolu Agency (republished in The Express Tribune)
aa-openai-math.note: OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts / 372 sets of results on GitHub on 6 October 2026. The IAS Math & AI advisory group said its advisory role is not an endorsement of the results.

deepmind-imo-2025.title: Advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think officially achieves gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad
deepmind-imo-2025.note: Quotes IMO President Gregor Dolinar confirming the gold-medal score; the work was done in plain language within 4.5 hours.

afp-jacobian.title: Formal Verification of an Explicit Counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture
afp-jacobian.publisher: Archive of Formal Proofs (Ramos, Hulak, de Queiroz)
afp-jacobian.note: Independent Isabelle/HOL check of the 3-dimensional map published by Levent Alpöge, crediting Claude Fable and Akhil Mathew (who posed the question). The 2-dimensional case remains open. The conjecture was posed by Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939.

lean-lang.title: Lean — programming language and proof assistant
lean-lang.note: Lean is an open-source programming language and proof assistant.

willison-openai-imo.title: OpenAI's gold medal performance on the International Math Olympiad
willison-openai-imo.note: Summary of Alexander Wei's (OpenAI) announcement: an experimental model, 5 of 6 problems, graded by three former IMO medallists; OpenAI's own assessment, not official IMO grading.
